title: The Danger of Overreaching as a Leader
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This essay examines leaders who extend their authority beyond appropriate boundaries, tracing the behavior to arrogance, self-interest, and a belief that the ends justify the means. It argues overreaching leaders systematically underestimate resistance and dismiss cautionary advice from trusted advisors, and that the pattern appears across governments, corporations, militaries, nonprofits, and even families. The piece identifies observable warning signs — controlling communication, refusing to delegate even minor tasks, denying access to information, rejecting feedback — and argues preventing overreach requires courageous colleagues to unite in flagging the danger together, since individual pushback rarely succeeds against a leader already inclined to overreach.
points: Ties overreaching to a specific psychological profile: arrogance, dominance, and belief that the ends justify the means.
Argues overreaching leaders systematically underestimate resistance and dismiss cautionary advice from trusted advisors.
Notes the pattern appears across governments, corporations, militaries, nonprofits, and families — not just high-profile political examples.
Lists concrete observable warning signs: controlling communication, refusing to delegate minor tasks, denying access to information, rejecting feedback.
Argues prevention requires multiple colleagues acting in unison, since individual pushback rarely succeeds against an already-overreaching leader.
quotes: A leader who extends their authority or influence beyond acceptable limits is said to be “overreaching.
Leaders who overreach often alienate their colleagues, leading to conflict and an erosion of credibility and trust.
Because they believe the “ends justify the means,” they convince themselves that people will get over their discomfort once they realize the benefits of the leader’s choices.

Look for leaders who control communication, refuse to delegate even minor tasks, deny access to data or information that describes the current state, and refuse feedback or criticism. These are leaders likely to overreach sometime soon.

This works best when they hold hands together and surround the leader with a common view that going too far is perilous. The more team members who can carry this message in unison, the greater the odds of preventing the overreach.
